content.title: Global Renewable Energy Landscape
content.intro: M8: Renewable Energy Technologies and Innovations

content.text: This lesson explores the rapid advancements in renewable energy technologies and their role in reshaping global energy systems. It highlights the increasing adoption of renewables due to technological innovation and declining costs, alongside significant regional disparities in electricity generation and access. This lesson demonstrates that despite progress, challenges such as financial gaps, energy storage limitations, and infrastructural barriers persist. The lesson underscores the urgent need for collaborative efforts and investments to ensure a just and inclusive transition to sustainable energy.

content.title: Key Concepts
content.intro: Explore foundational ideas from this lesson.

content.text: The renewable energy technology landscape is evolving rapidly due the urgent need to combat climate change, reduce reliance on fossil fuels, and provide universal access to affordable, reliable, and sustainable energy. As of 2022, renewable energy accounted for 28.2% of global electricity consumption, with solar, wind, and hydropower leading the charge. This transformation reflects a combination of technological innovation, declining costs, and supportive policies, positioning renewables as the fastest-growing segment of the global energy market.

content.intro: M8: Renewable Energy Technologies and Innovations
content.title: Part 1: Advancements in Renewable Energy Technologies

content.text: Key advancements have propelled renewable energy technologies to the forefront. Solar photovoltaic (PV) costs, for instance, have dropped by 89% since 2010, making solar the most cost-competitive energy source in many regions.

Wind energy has seen similar growth, with cutting-edge turbines now capable of generating up to 15 MW per unit, enabling large-scale deployment even in moderate wind areas. Global investment in renewable technologies reached $495 billion in 2022, reflecting both progress and the persistent disparity in clean energy financing; over 80% of these investments remain concentrated in just 25 countries, underscoring the inequities faced by low-income nations.

Energy storage and grid integration technologies have undergone significant innovation.

Battery storage capacity expanded by over 50% in 2022, reaching 16 GW globally, providing critical solutions to the intermittency challenges of solar and wind power. The rise of green hydrogen, a renewable alternative for industrial and transportation applications, marks another transformative shift. Costs for hydrogen production from renewables have dropped by over 60% in the past decade, with projections indicating further reductions as deployment scales up.

However, this landscape also reveals persistent challenges. Nearly 685 million people globally still lack access to electricity, while over 2.1 billion people rely on polluting fuels for cooking, resulting in 3.2 million premature deaths annually. In Sub-Saharan Africa, where over 570 million people live without electricity, decentralized solutions like solar mini-grids and home systems represent untapped potential but face financial and infrastructural hurdles. Furthermore, achieving universal energy access and climate targets requires mobilizing annual investments of $770 billion—a figure far exceeding current levels.

The rapid pace of technological advancements in renewable energy provides an unprecedented opportunity to reshape global energy systems. By leveraging innovation and addressing systemic inequities and creating an enabling environment, renewable energy technologies can drive a just and inclusive energy transition, reducing greenhouse gas emissions, fostering economic growth, and improving the quality of life for millions worldwide. The next decade will be pivotal in determining whether the promise of renewable energy can be fully realized to meet the twin imperatives of climate action and sustainable development.

content.intro: M8: Renewable Energy Technologies and Innovations
content.title: Part 2: Renewable electricity generation by region

content.text:
In absolute terms of renewable electricity generation, Asia led the world in 2022, generating 3 749 TWh, a 9.3% increase driven by solar and hydropower, both offsetting declines in wind energy and bioenergy.

North America came in second for the first time, with 1 493 TWh, up by 8.6% across energy sources, despite a drop in bioenergy. Europe generated 1 462 TWh a small 0.6% decrease from 2021. South America generated 940 TWh, showing an 11.9% increase from 2021 due to a hydropower recovery and a greater role of solar energy.

Eurasia produced 363 TWh, growing slightly by 2.5%, with solar and wind making up for continuous declines in hydropower. Africa generated 205 TWh, showing a modest growth of 3.5% across all sources. Oceania generated 125 TWh, a robust 14.1% increase across energy sources. Central America and the Caribbean followed with 57 TWh with a 1.3% growth. Lastly, the Middle East generated 47 TWh, seeing a 16.9% rise due to new wind energy additions and ongoing solar expansion.

In terms of the electricity mix by region, South America leads the way with 75.0% of its electricity coming from renewable sources, predominantly hydropower, which accounts for three-quarters of their renewable energy.

Europe follows with 40.5% of its electricity from renewables, characterized by a more varied mix:
35.7% wind energy, 33.3% hydropower, 16.1% solar, 14.0% bioenergy and 0.8% geothermal. Central America and the Caribbean, along with Oceania, both generate close to 38% of their electricity from renewables.

In North America, renewables contribute to 27.0% of the electricity mix, while in Asia, the figure is 26.2%. Eurasia had 23.5% renewable electricity, while Africa had 22.8%. Lastly, the Middle East lags significantly behind, with just 3.4% of its electricity generated from renewables.

The G20 and G7 countries generated mostly non-renewable electricity in 2022 and less renewable electricity than the global 29.1%. G20 countries produced 28.9% of their electricity with renewable sources, while the G7 generated 28.5% renewable electricity. Both groups have similar breakdowns in renewable sources. Out of all renewable electricity generated in 2022, G20 countries had 46.3% hydropower, 28.4% wind energy, 16.5% solar energy, 7.9% bioenergy and traces of geothermal energy. G7 countries had 36.6% hydropower, 33.1% wind energy, 18.0% solar energy, 9.5% bioenergy and 1.2% of geothermal energy.

content.title: Key Takeaways
content.intro: If you only have space to remember 3 things:

takeaways.title: Monitoring progress towards sustainable energy goals is key.
takeaways.description: Monitoring the evolution of key indicators, such as the renewable energy share in total final energy consumption (e.g., indicator 7.2.1), provides vital insights into the progress toward sustainable energy goals. This data-driven approach enhances countries' ability to plan scenarios effectively in line with achieving global energy targets by 2030.

takeaways.title: Economic growth and energy policies are critical.
takeaways.description: Data-driven analysis offers valuable evidence regarding the economic impacts of different energy policies, including effects on GDP, employment rates, and trade balances. Energy modellling, encompassing various methodologies such as econometric analysis and technology-rich accounting frameworks, serves as a crucial component in informing energy policy formulation.

takeaways.title: We must always be evaluating the environmental impact of sustainable energy development.
takeaways.description: Integration of data on sustainable energy development with environmental datasets enables comprehensive assessments of environmental impacts and facilitates the monitoring of changes over time.
